title: What’s happened to the global rules-based order?
author: Stephen Grenville
text: |United States, explained.Economist John Maynard Keynes (centre) played a leading role in the formulation of the Bretton Woods agreements and establishment of the International Monetary Fund (Hulton Archive/Getty Images)What’s happened to the global rules-based order?Trump’s tariffs bruise trade, but self-interest keeps economic cooperation largely intact.Stephen Grenville4 November 20265 min read|What’s happened to the global rules-based order?What’s happened to the global rules-based order?A recent dialogue between Sam Roggeveen and John Edwards (Opens in new window) on John’s new Lowy Institute Paper (Opens in new window) Overhaul: How Australia can adapt to a changing world economy highlights different perceptions about the much-vaunted “global rules-based order”. For some (particularly those focused on international relations and security issues), the rules are like the stone tablets brought down from the mountain. For them, Trump’s assault on trade is a game-changer (Opens in new window). For others – especially economists – the rules are an amorphous accumulation of agreements and understandings which facilitate international interactions. These will adapt to the assault to minimise the damage.It is understandable that some see the rules-based order as being a manifestation of America’s unassailed power after the Second World War, associated with the 1944 Bretton Woods conference. America force-marched the dismantling of colonial empires (with their restrictive trade relationships favouring the home country) and created a presumption for free trade through tariff-reducing negotiations under GATT (the precursor to the World Trade Organisation). With the IMF fixed exchange rates regime replacing the gold standard, countries would no longer have to constrain imports and growth to maintain their scarce gold holdings, which had been so damaging to global trade in the 1930s.What followed was an extraordinary burgeoning of globalisation. The usual metric – world trade (imports and exports) as a percent of GDP – rose from 15% in 1950 to almost 60% in 2024. At least as important was international investment (growing from almost nothing following the Second World War to around 5% of GDP in 2007), which transferred managerial and technical knowhow, as well as financing. Advances in communications and transport (notably containerised shipping) sped the process along.Economists agree that this globalisation was hugely beneficial for growth and living standards. But they argue that much of this would have happened without any hegemon orchestrating the process or enforcing the rules (Opens in new window). The Bretton Woods fixed exchange rates didn’t come into practical effect until the late 1950s, and largely broke down within a decade, with the final nail hammered home by President Nixon’s ending of gold convertibility in 1971. Successive GATT rounds of tariff reduction ran out of steam, even beforethe failed Doha Round in 2001.ResearchOverhaul: How Australia can adapt to a changing world economyRead lowy institute paperGlobalisation grew even as the Bretton Woods institutions atrophied. The enabling environment pre-dated the system (with substantial globalisation before the Second World War) and didn’t end with its effective demise.Long before Bretton Woods, there had been agreed rules between countries to facilitate economic interaction. These continue, modified and augmented, to this day. These rules cover marine trade, aviation, communications, intellectual property, health and sanitary standards, space, pollution and myriad other issues. The economic-oriented agreements sit comfortably alongside other international agreements, such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), covering international boundaries.Developing and maintaining such rules relies on both parties benefitting, otherwise they will not sign up. This doesn’t mean that both parties benefit equally or equitably; but there must be a negotiating process which ensures mutual gains.Global trade is intrinsically win-win (economists talk confidently of “the gains from trade”), not the zero-sum tussle Trump envisages. Countries shouldn’t need much encouragement for free trade, which is almost always in the interests of both parties. Retaliating to tariffs imposed by other countries is “like putting rocks in your own harbour (Opens in new window)”.While the benefits of free trade are one of the few topics on which economists agree, the wider public has never been convinced. Expanding globalisation was accompanied by a constant background babble of disagreement, illustrated by demonstrations against the WTO in Seattle in 1999. In America, the Democrats are dubious about free trade.Nor have countries honoured the central principle of the GATT and WTO: the so-called “most-favoured nation”. This actually requires countries not to have a most-favoured nation – to treat all countries alike. In practice, blocs such as the European Union discriminate against outsiders and maintain substantial protection for politically favoured agriculture. In more recent years, so-called “free-trade” agreements (actually preferential discriminatory arrangements) have become common.Nevertheless, international trade grew faster than GDP until 2008, and since then has kept pace.Trump has, however, brought a crucial change: the overt and frequent use of economic instruments to pursue security goals. Of course this is not new, but Trump sees tariffs as his primary coercive tool. This is now a dominant overlay on all international relations. Security and supply resilience are now used to justify trade-distorting industrial policies subsidising domestic production. Further distortion comes through “friend-shoring” (Opens in new window), designed to secure supply. Policy routinely includes the use of “chokepoints” (Opens in new window) – export controls, sanctions, boycotts, travel bans and limits on the use of American financial infrastructure.Australia will not stop trading with China, whatever America threatens.How will this work out?Trade finds a way around barriers, like flowing water. American attempts to restrict Chinese imports have rerouted trade via intermediaries. Trump’s efforts confirm that tariffs mainly harm the country imposing them. Most of the economic rules are self-policing, self-adjusting and maintained by the powerful incentivising force of mutual self-interest. While international coordination via institutions like the WTO has been valuable, many agreements don’t require universal participation: a smaller like-minded group can often find useful alignment. Market-based exchange rates seem to work satisfactorily, with little intervention. Trump is a mercantilist, disliking imports and current account deficits. But he does not favour autarky and welcomes foreign investment. China seeks the option of self-sufficiency (Opens in new window) but still has high imports (nearly 20% of GDP) for such a large country. History suggests that sanctions and financial restrictions have only a temporary impact (Opens in new window), as work-around measures evolve. Some fear that security considerations will fracture global trade into self-sufficient blocs (Opens in new window), but the enormous economic penalty from such a transformation argues against it happening. Australia will not stop trading with China, whatever America threatens.Beyond international trade, the damage may be greater. Not all international interactions are motivated (and maintained) by self-interest. International aid, humanitarian efforts and refugee programs have been weakened. Collective-action challenges (the “tragedy of the commons” (Opens in new window)), notably efforts to contain climate change, benefit from a coordinating hegemon, so Trump’s departure from the Paris Accord is a serious blow. Some issues – like mining the seabed – pit environmental arguments against commercial advantage and may be resolved by power rather than rational analysis.There are policy implications here (Opens in new window). The most obvious one, for a country like Australia, is to do whatever it can to maintain the openness that has served it so well – avoiding special exclusive trade relationships and remaining open to investment from all (Opens in new window). The central principle of the WTO – avoiding a “most favoured nation” – is still good guidance. But to mourn the passing of the specific rules hammered out at Bretton Woods is a distraction from today’s international challenges.About the authorStephen GrenvilleDr Grenville is a Nonresident Fellow at the Lowy Institute.TopicsUnited StatesEconomyWorld Trade OrganisationTrade & investmentThe Interpreter on United StatesExplore The InterpreterUnited StatesTrump lost the midterms – not his grip on foreign policy5 November 2026Cory AlpertVietnamVietnam’s other trade deals could claim Washington’s wins4 November 2026Tran Hoang Tu Linh G20The G20 under Trump: The impact of a leaner agenda 4 November 2026Abhinandan KumarMore on United StatesExplore United StatesResearchAsia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominanceData Snapshot by Jack Sato, Hunter MarstonResearchIndia-Australia defence ties: Advancing a vital Indo-Pacific partnershipPolicy Brief by Dhruva JaishankarConversationsWhy the world economy could double again by 2050Sam Roggeveen, John EdwardsResearchOverhaul: How Australia can adapt to a changing world economyLowy Institute Paper by John Edwards
